summary:
SPHEREx is mapping the entire sky in infrared light, producing far more data than any one person can sift through. Project Stargazer makes that data something you can explore. Enter a sky position, or start with a challenge target like WISE 0855, and Stargazer pulls real observations from NASA’s archive, aligns them, and lets you scrub or play through them over time to see what moves.


Compare detector bands, check the wavelength of each exposure, and click any source to build its spectrum. Then listen to it: Stargazer turns each spectrum into sound, so you can hear how an object’s brightness changes across infrared wavelengths. Every view has a shareable link, and a built-in space lets users discuss what they find.

By making the sky easier to see, and to hear, Stargazer helps more people, including blind and low-vision users, take part in spotting patterns worth a closer look.
details:
Introduction

Project Stargazer is a web app for exploring real SPHEREx infrared observations. The goal behind it is simple: anyone should be able to use it, whether they’re a student, a hobbyist, a volunteer, or a person who has low vision or is color blind.

Most astronomy tools I’ve come across lean heavily on images and color, which quietly leaves people out. SPHEREx is mapping the whole sky, and the challenge asks for a public tool to help people spot what changes. If the public is the audience, the tool has to work for the whole public. So accessibility is the main idea of this project, and every feature below is built around it.

What it does

You type in a sky position (decimal degrees or RA/Dec) or choose a preset: WISE 0855, Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae, R Draconis, or the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS. Press Load observations and the Python server asks NASA’s IRSA archive for every matching SPHEREx exposure. It downloads small FITS cutouts, lines them up on one sky grid centered on your target, and sends them to your browser as images.

From there you can:

  • Scrub through exposures in time order with a single slider, Previous/Next buttons, or autoplay at 0.5×, 1×, 2× or 4×.
  • Blink between the first and last exposure, the classic trick for seeing what moved.
  • Choose a detector band (D1 to D6, roughly 0.75 to 5.00 µm) or load all six.
  • Switch the image mode: grayscale, a band tint, or a false-color composite. The composite is display-only, and the app says so.
  • Set the field of view anywhere from 0.01° to 1.00° (though queries >0.20° seems to face issues from time to time), with a crosshair, north/east cues and a scale bar.
  • Open an Aladin Lite reference sky for the same position.
  • Choose how much to download to CSV; a quick preview (up to eight frames spread across time), every available observation, or a date range.

Then comes my favourite (and most technically challenging) part. Click anywhere on an image and Stargazer measures a spectrum at that spot. The server maps your click to sky coordinates, tries to match a unique Gaia DR3 source, and follows that source’s proper motion from exposure to exposure. It does aperture photometry on each frame (a 2-pixel aperture, with background taken from a 4 to 7 pixel ring) and returns wavelength-sorted points with uncertainties and quality flags.

"Built for the public, with accessibility first". Thus, accessibility is taken really really seriously.

Accessibility Implementations

You can hear the data

Charts are hard to use without good vision, so Stargazer also plays the spectrum as sound. Measurements play in order of increasing wavelength as short synthesized notes. Wavelength sets the pitch on a log scale, and flux sets the volume across the measured range. An optional setting turns measurement uncertainty into vibrato, so a shaky data point sounds shaky. Each note highlights its point on the chart, so sighted users can follow along, and playback can be stopped at any time.

It’s an extra way to read the same data. Someone who can’t read a plot can still tell a rising spectrum from a flat one, and sighted users hear things they might have skimmed past.

Charts are never the only way in

  • Every spectrum comes with an expandable data table of the actual measured values, each with a button to jump to its source frame.
  • The measurements-over-time plot (date against approximate wavelength) has its own selection controls, an inspector, and a matching table.
  • Spectrum points are focusable and usable from the keyboard. Hovering or tabbing to a point shows its wavelength, flux, uncertainty, detector, date, frame and quality, and pressing Enter takes you to that exposure.
  • The wide spectrum chart scrolls horizontally with the keyboard or a trackpad.
  • Results can be downloaded as CSV, so people can use their own tools, such as a screen-reader-friendly spreadsheet.

Shapes and labels as Accessibility Tools

Detector bands are shown with labels and shapes as well as color. A color-blind-friendly chart palette is one setting away, and points with quality flags are visually distinct from clean ones. If you can’t tell two shades apart, you can still tell which band you’re looking at.

A dedicated settings page, shared across all public pages, lets people tailor the interface:

  • Text size from 100% to 200% in 10% steps
  • High contrast for text, surfaces, borders and focus indicators
  • Larger buttons and form controls
  • A motion setting that follows your operating system or can be set to reduced or allowed, with optional reveal animations on pages
  • Live preview and one-click reset

These preferences are saved in your browser only. They aren’t uploaded and they don’t end up in share links, so changing how the page looks never changes what you send to someone else.

Keyboard and assistive technology basics

Pages have skip links, semantic headings and labels, visible keyboard focus, live status updates (so search progress is announced), and accessible names on controls.

Embeds

An embeddable viewer that other websites, museums or classrooms could drop into a page using the same URL parameters.

A direct line for feedback

Accessibility problems are easiest to find when the people affected can report them. Anyone, without signing in, can send an anonymous accessibility report of up to 4,000 characters. It contains only the message and the time it was sent, with no visual preferences attached. Reports are stored privately on the server and aren’t publicly readable.

Community Collaboration

Anyone can read the Community discussions without an account. Signing in is only needed to post or reply. Posts can attach the exact observation context (target, coordinates, band, field of view, exposure time, wavelength), and readers can open that field in the explorer with one click, so questions about a specific field come with the data. Rich text formatting, attaching files, mentioning users are all supported. Posts also comes with tags so that users can search for what they're looking for.

Note: Filters for sensitive contents are still not implemented in this version. Behaviours in the Community Discussions page are not automatically regulated... Worrying... :(

Benefits and intended impact

SPHEREx is producing more images than any one person can examine. The challenge brief points out that volunteers have helped discover most known comets and brown dwarfs by comparing images over time. That only scales if more kinds of people can take part.

Stargazer aims to:

  1. Remove the technical barrier. No FITS software, no scripting, and no archive knowledge are needed.
  2. Remove the sensory barrier. The same data can be seen, read in a table, or heard.
  3. Make discoveries shareable. Links, community posts and attached observation context let people point each other at something worth a second look.
  4. Teach by doing. Anyone can look at a real object like Barnard’s Star or WISE 0855, play its exposures, and see its spectrum for themselves.

Tools and technology

  • Python backend: server.py runs the web service, background jobs, caching, and the community, account and accessibility-report APIs.
  • Data processing: spherex_processing.py reads the FITS science, flag, zodiacal-light and wavelength extensions. It masks bad pixels, optionally subtracts the zodiacal model, reprojects onto a target-centered celestial grid, and renders PNG frames with an asinh display stretch.
  • Offline tooling: scripts/build_spherex_stack.py builds stacks from FITS files already on disk, and notebooks support data validation.
  • Data sources: NASA/IPAC IRSA SIA2 (spherex_dr1 and spherex_qr3 collections) and Gaia DR3.
  • Front end: a responsive browser interface, with Aladin Lite as an optional reference panel.
  • Performance: cutouts download in parallel (up to four at a time) with one automatic retry, frames load on demand instead of all at once, and a server cache keyed to position, field size, band and settings means repeat searches are instant.
  • Hardware: just a regular computer running the server and a web browser.
  • Configuration: host, port and cache location are set with environment variables.
  • Artificial Intelligence: Artificial Intelligence was use for debugging and quality checks. It is also utilized for emotional support during desperate times.

Inspiration & Considerations

The idea of putting image, spectrum and sound in one place is where the project gets its character. You see a faint dot drift across a field, click it, get a spectrum, and listen to it, without leaving the page. The sound doesn’t replace the chart or the pictures. It’s a third way to read the data, built for people who are usually left out of this field.

What I considered along the way:

Honesty

  • Stargazer does not detect or confirm moving objects. It helps people compare real exposures and decide for themselves. When IRSA has no coverage, the app says so, and no simulated frames are ever shown as a fallback.
  • Points are never connected across gaps. Skipped exposures are reported with the reason. Wavelengths come from an approximate lookup and fluxes have no PSF correction, so spectra are labeled exploratory, not science-grade.
  • Median stacking is intentionally turned off because the matched spectral calibration products aren’t loaded yet - due to time constraints :*(. Image brightness is stretched per frame, so it shouldn’t be compared across dates or bands.
  • The RGB composite and band tints are labeled as false color, not visible-light color, so nobody mistakes them for photographs.

Privacy

  • Visual settings stay in the browser, accessibility reports are anonymous and private, and browser history stays on the user’s device.

Reuse and speed

  • Caching history (up to 50 searches) and on-demand frame loading keep the app usable for people on slower connections or machines, so that sharing or quering an observation that has already been done will be instant.

Future Implementation Ideas

These are the things I’d build next, with no time constraints:


1. Better, more trustworthy science

  • Right now wavelengths come from an approximate WCS-WAVE lookup, and fluxes have no PSF correction. The next step is to load the matched CWAVE and CBAND calibration products and add an aperture correction, so spectra move from “exploratory” toward something researchers can trust.
  • Implementing median stacking. Ahhhh, due to time constraints I couldn't add this. I really wanted to add this...
  • The blink control shows two frames, but it doesn’t compute what changed. A calibrated difference view would make the faint changes easier to notice.
  • Overlays from other surveys. Gaia is already used behind the scenes to follow proper motion, so showing known catalog sources on the image could be nice.
  • Stargazer will never confirm a moving object on its own, and I want to keep it that way. But it could let people mark a possible mover, show where several users agree, and label it as a candidate, not a detection. That’s close to how volunteer projects work.

2. Going further on accessibility

This is the part I care about most, and honestly the part with the most room left.

  • Test with real people. The features exist, but I haven’t yet run structured testing with screen-reader users, people who are blind or have low vision, or people with different kinds of color blindness. I’d like to run those sessions, fix what breaks, and publish what I learned.
  • A formal accessibility audit against WCAG, so claims about the app can be backed by something checkable.
  • Plain-language descriptions of images and spectra. A short generated summary like “the source brightens toward longer wavelengths” would help people who can’t see the plot or the picture, and it would help beginners too.
  • More ways to hear the data. Sonification currently plays a spectrum as a sweep of notes. Some ideas I’d try: a chord mode that plays all bands at once, a time mode that turns brightness over dates into sound (useful for variable stars like RW Aurigae and R Draconis), and a short audio cue when the playback moves to a new frame.
  • Multiple languages.
  • Better support for small screens and slower connections, including a lighter mode that loads smaller images.

3. Community and learning

  • Ready-made exercises using the six featured targets, so a teacher can set “find what moves in this field” as an activity in classrooms.
  • Beginner guides inside the app.
  • Moderation and safety tools for the community area, such as reporting posts, as it grows.
  • Better threads. Following a discussion, notifications for replies (mentions already work), and links from a post straight to the exact frame it describes.

4. Reaching the public for real

  • Today Stargazer runs from one server. Making it truly public means a hosted site with HTTPS, persistent storage and backups.

Hopes and Dreams

I started this project because I kept running into the same problem. Space is something everyone feels they’re allowed to love, but the tools for actually exploring it assume you can see small details, tell colours apart, read dense charts, and already know your way around the data. A lot of people, including me, gets pushed away before they even begin.

SPHEREx is going to photograph the entire sky again and again. It’s too much for any one person, or even any one team, to look through. I hope Stargazer helps make that job feel shared.

I hope someone who has never opened a scientific data file can type in a star’s name, press play, and watch the sky shift, and feel the small thrill of “wait, that dot moved.”

I hope someone with low vision or colour blindness can use the same tool as everyone else, without needing a workaround, and without feeling like an afterthought. And I hope someone who can’t see the chart at all can listen to a spectrum and still get something real out of it.

I hope a teacher can put this in front of a class and have it just work.

I hope a volunteer might one day notice something worth a closer look, and that a professional astronomer will take that seriously. Stargazer doesn’t claim to discover anything by itself. It only tries to help more people look, and look carefully.

I also hope this project is honest. I chose to say “no coverage” instead of showing fake frames, to label spectra as exploratory, and to leave out features I couldn’t back up. If people trust what Stargazer tells them, then they can build on it.

Mostly, I hope accessibility stops being a feature that gets added at the end of astronomy tools and becomes the starting point. If Stargazer is a small example of that, then it did its job.
